claims.text: NiTi shape-memory alloys exhibit pronounced temperature-dependent plastic deformation behavior.
The reversible martensitic-to-austenitic transformation alters the dominant deformation mechanisms in NiTi.
NiTi is martensitic at temperatures below its transformation range.
Low-temperature martensitic NiTi exhibits typical pseudoelastic behavior.
Sweeping temperature from below the martensitic-finish temperature to above the austenitic-finish temperature traverses the NiTi phase-transformation range.
Temperature changes produce martensite-austenite phase boundaries in NiTi.
Martensite-austenite phase boundaries modify dislocation mobility.
Martensite-austenite phase boundaries promote transformation-induced plasticity.
At lower temperatures, twinned martensitic NiTi deforms primarily by variant reorientation.
Dislocation slip in low-temperature martensitic NiTi is limited.
At higher temperatures, austenite governs plastic deformation in NiTi.
Austenitic NiTi has higher dislocation mobility than martensitic NiTi.
The reversible phase transformation provides a tunable microstructural pathway correlated with temperature-dependent yield and plastic strain.
Yield strength varies markedly across the NiTi transformation-temperature range.
The dominant deformation mode transitions from twinning and variant reorientation in martensite to dislocation-based plasticity in austenite.
NiTi yield strength and ductility have a predictable nonlinear dependence on temperature.
At fixed room temperature, NiTi predominantly exhibits pseudoelastic behavior without temperature-induced phase transitions.
The proposed behavior is limited to the temperature window bounded by the martensitic-finish and austenitic-finish temperatures.
Alloy composition, processing history, testing rate, and dislocation interactions may affect the magnitude of the temperature-dependent response.
